title: TCP, UDP, QUIC and HTTP/1.1, 2, 3 for designers
scopeHtml: Scope: TCP handshake, reliability and congestion control, head-of-line blocking, UDP, QUIC, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and how to choose protocols and timeouts. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: TCP in plain words
notes.html:
TCP gives two programs a reliable, ordered stream of bytes over an unreliable network. The internet itself only moves loose packets that can be lost, duplicated or reordered. TCP numbers every byte, the receiver acknowledges what it got, and the sender resends what is missing.

Starting a connection is the three-way handshake: client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client sends ACK. That is 1 round trip (RTT) before the first data byte can be sent (the client can send data with its ACK). Closing uses FIN/ACK in each direction, and the side that closes first sits in TIME_WAIT (commonly 60 s on Linux) so late packets do not confuse a new connection.

Client                      Server
  | ---- SYN (seq=x) ------> |
  | <--- SYN-ACK (y, x+1) -- |    1 RTT
  | ---- ACK (y+1) + data -> |

Worked example. RTT Mumbai to Virginia is about 200 ms. A fresh connection spends 200 ms in the handshake before sending anything. A mobile app that opens a new connection per request pays this every time; one that reuses a connection pays it once.

Industry examples. Every database driver uses a connection pool (HikariCP, pgbouncer) mostly to avoid this setup cost, plus per-connection memory on the server (Postgres uses a process per connection, about 5 to 10 MB each).

Everyday analogy. A phone call: "Hello?" "Hello, who is this?" "It's me." Only then do you start talking, and you hang up politely at the end.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the handshake RTT when computing latency.
  • Not knowing TIME_WAIT: thousands of short outbound connections can exhaust local ports (ephemeral range about 28k ports by default, net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range).
  • Saying TCP is "faster" than UDP. It is more reliable, not faster.

notes.title: TCP reliability, flow control and congestion control
notes.html:
Three separate mechanisms, often confused.

  1. Reliability: sequence numbers plus ACKs plus retransmit timers. Fast retransmit resends after 3 duplicate ACKs, without waiting for the timeout.
  2. Flow control: the receiver advertises a window (how much buffer it has left) so a fast sender does not drown a slow receiver. Protects the receiver.
  3. Congestion control: the sender limits itself by a congestion window (cwnd) to avoid overloading the network. It starts small (slow start: initial cwnd of 10 segments, about 14 KB, doubling every RTT) and then grows slowly; on packet loss it shrinks. Algorithms: Reno, CUBIC (Linux default), BBR (Google, models bandwidth and RTT instead of reacting to loss).

Worked example. Fetching 1 MB over a fresh connection with RTT 100 ms: slow start sends 14 KB, then 28, 56, 112, 224, 448 KB... roughly 6 round trips to deliver 1 MB, so about 600 ms plus handshake, even on a 1 Gbps link. Bandwidth is not the limit, round trips are. This is why small pages, early connection reuse and CDNs near the user matter. Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth x RTT: 100 Mbps x 100 ms = 1.25 MB must be "in flight" to fill the pipe, so windows must be large enough (window scaling).

Industry examples. Google deployed BBR on YouTube and google.com, reporting throughput gains on lossy long links. CDNs tune initial cwnd and use TCP tuning for large video chunks.

Decision gravity. Changing congestion control (sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr) is a reversible per-host setting, but behaves differently with other flows on shared links; test it.

Everyday analogy. Filling a bucket through a pipe: flow control is "the bucket says it is almost full", congestion control is "the pipe in the street is jammed, trickle slowly and speed up carefully".

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up flow control (receiver) and congestion control (network).
  • Thinking more bandwidth fixes slow downloads on high-latency links.
  • Forgetting slow start restarts after idle periods unless disabled (tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0).

notes.title: Head-of-line blocking and TCP's limits
notes.html:
TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, so one lost packet blocks everything behind it until it is resent. This is head-of-line (HOL) blocking at the transport layer. If you multiplex 10 requests over one TCP connection (HTTP/2) and one packet is lost, all 10 streams stall waiting for the retransmit, although only one stream owned the lost packet.

Other TCP limits for designers: the handshake RTT, slow start per connection, the connection is tied to the IP:port 4-tuple (a phone switching from Wi-Fi to 4G breaks it), and the protocol is baked into operating system kernels and middleboxes, so it is very hard to change.

Worked example. 2% packet loss on a mobile network, RTT 80 ms. Each loss costs at least 1 RTT (fast retransmit), more with timeout (200 ms or more). On HTTP/2 over TCP, loss stalls all parallel streams; on HTTP/3 only the affected stream waits. Measured gains of HTTP/3 are largest on poor networks.

Industry examples. This was the key motivation for QUIC at Google and for HTTP/3 deployment at Cloudflare, Meta and Google. Meta reported lower request errors and tail latency with QUIC in their mobile apps.

Everyday analogy. A single-lane road: one broken-down car holds up all the cars behind, even those going to different towns.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing HTTP/2 removed head-of-line blocking entirely. It removed it at the HTTP layer only.
  • Not realising a connection breaks when the client IP changes.

notes.title: UDP and when to use it
notes.html:
UDP just sends a packet and does not care what happens next. No handshake, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control. Header is 8 bytes versus 20 or more for TCP. The application adds whatever reliability it needs.

Good for: DNS (one request, one reply), live video and voice (an old frame is useless, so do not wait for a resend), games, metrics (StatsD), service discovery, and as the base for QUIC and WebRTC. Bad for: anything where you need every byte in order unless you build it yourself.

         TCP                          UDP
 handshake, ordered, retransmit    fire and forget, 8-byte header
 one stream of bytes               independent datagrams
 congestion controlled             you must control rate yourself

Worked example. A game sending position updates 30 times per second. If packet 17 is lost, TCP would stall packets 18 to 20 until 17 is resent (about 1 RTT); UDP simply uses packet 18, a fresher update. Packet size: keep under about 1,200 to 1,400 bytes to avoid IP fragmentation (MTU 1,500 typical; QUIC uses a minimum 1,200 bytes).

Industry examples. DNS, NTP, DHCP, Zoom/Meet/WebRTC media, Statsd/Datadog agent metrics, Valve game servers, and QUIC underlying HTTP/3.

Decision gravity. Choosing UDP means you own reliability and congestion fairness: powerful but expensive in engineering. Usually you adopt QUIC or an existing protocol rather than invent one. Reversible only if clients can be updated.

Everyday analogy. Dropping postcards in a letterbox versus registered courier: postcards are cheap and fast, but some never arrive.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying UDP is "unreliable so never use it". Many critical systems use it on purpose.
  • Sending large UDP datagrams that get fragmented and silently dropped.
  • Forgetting UDP has no congestion control, so a flood can hurt others.

notes.title: QUIC
notes.html:
QUIC is a modern transport built on UDP that gives you TCP-like reliability, TLS 1.3 security and multiple independent streams in one protocol. It runs in user space (app/library), so it can evolve quickly, unlike kernel TCP. It is the transport of HTTP/3.

What it fixes:

  • Faster setup: transport and TLS handshake are combined: 1 RTT for a new connection, 0-RTT to a server you have talked to before (data sent in the first flight, with replay-attack risk, so only for idempotent requests).
  • No cross-stream HOL blocking: each stream has its own ordering; loss on one stream does not stall others.
  • Connection migration: a connection is identified by a connection ID, not the IP:port, so a phone moving from Wi-Fi to 4G keeps the same connection.
  • Always encrypted, including most headers, which also stops middleboxes from ossifying the protocol.

Costs: more CPU (user-space packet handling, encryption per packet; early reports of 2x CPU versus TCP), some networks block or throttle UDP 443 so clients must fall back to TCP, and load balancers need QUIC awareness (route by connection ID).

Worked example. RTT 100 ms. HTTP/2 over TCP + TLS 1.3 on a new connection: 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) = 200 ms before the request. HTTP/3: 1 RTT = 100 ms. On a resumed connection with 0-RTT: 0 ms of setup, request goes out immediately.

Industry examples. Google invented it (gQUIC) and standardised it as RFC 9000 in 2021. Cloudflare, Fastly, Meta, YouTube and Cloudflare-fronted sites serve large shares of traffic over HTTP/3. Nginx and Envoy support it; many origins still use HTTP/1.1 or 2 behind the CDN.

Decision gravity. Enabling HTTP/3 at the CDN edge is cheap and reversible (clients fall back). Running QUIC end to end internally costs CPU and tooling maturity; most teams keep it at the edge only.

Everyday analogy. A shipping container that already contains separate boxes and a lock: one trip delivers several independent parcels, and if you change lorries the container keeps its tracking number.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying QUIC is "UDP so unreliable". QUIC adds its own reliability and congestion control.
  • Forgetting 0-RTT replay risk and the need for TCP fallback.
  • Ignoring that firewalls dropping UDP break it unless fallback exists.

notes.title: HTTP/1.1
notes.html:
HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, as text. Messages look like GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1, headers, blank line, body. Keep-Alive (default in 1.1) reuses the connection. Pipelining existed in theory but was broken in practice (still strict order, HOL at HTTP level), so browsers turned it off.

Because one connection handles one request at a time, browsers open about 6 parallel connections per host. Developers used workarounds: domain sharding (img1.site.com, img2.site.com), sprite sheets, file bundling. Headers (cookies, user agent) are repeated in full every request, often 500 B to several KB.

GET /api/orders/7 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.com
Accept: application/json
Connection: keep-alive

Worked example. A page with 60 small resources over HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections: 10 rounds of fetches. At 50 ms RTT that is about 500 ms of pure waiting even with a fast server. Hence bundling.

Industry examples. Still used for simple internal service calls, webhooks and many health checks. Stripe's and GitHub's public APIs work fine over 1.1; the connection pool size matters more than the protocol.

Everyday analogy. A shop counter with one customer at a time; to go faster you open several counters (connections).

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing keep-alive is the default and what happens when idle timeouts of server and load balancer disagree (client sends on a connection the server just closed, giving random resets; set client idle timeout lower than the LB idle timeout, e.g. AWS ALB default 60 s).
  • Confusing pipelining with multiplexing.

notes.title: HTTP/2
notes.html:
HTTP/2 sends many requests at once over one TCP connection using binary frames. Each request/response is a stream with an ID; frames from different streams are interleaved, so a slow response no longer blocks a fast one at the HTTP level.

Features:

  • Multiplexing: hundreds of concurrent streams on 1 connection (SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, commonly 100 to 128).
  • HPACK header compression: repeated headers become tiny references.
  • Binary framing, stream priorities (largely replaced), flow control per stream.
  • Server push: mostly deprecated; Chrome removed it.
  • Requires TLS in practice (browsers only do h2 over HTTPS, negotiated via ALPN).

Weakness: all streams ride one TCP connection, so TCP HOL blocking hurts (see above). Also one connection means one congestion window and, with L4 load balancers, one backend: a few heavy gRPC connections can pile on a single server, so use L7 balancing for gRPC.

Worked example. Same 60 resources, one connection, all requested at once: about 1 RTT after the handshake plus transfer time, so the 500 ms example becomes roughly 100 ms. Domain sharding now hurts (extra handshakes, lost shared compression).

Industry examples. gRPC is built on HTTP/2. Nginx, Envoy, CloudFront and ALB speak h2 to clients. Most major websites use it.

Decision gravity. Moving from 1.1 to 2 at the edge is reversible and mostly free. For internal gRPC, the choice (HTTP/2 + protobuf) shapes the whole service contract and is a one-way-ish door.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant with one waiter who takes all your orders at once and brings dishes as they are ready, instead of waiting for each plate to be finished.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming HTTP/2 solves head-of-line blocking completely.
  • Putting an L4 balancer in front of gRPC and getting lopsided load.
  • Still recommending bundling and domain sharding under h2.

notes.title: HTTP/3
notes.html:
HTTP/3 is HTTP semantics (same methods, headers, status codes) over QUIC instead of TCP. To your application code nothing changes; the difference is below.

Differences from HTTP/2: transport is QUIC/UDP, so no TCP HOL blocking; header compression is QPACK (redesigned to avoid blocking across streams); setup is 1 RTT or 0-RTT; connection survives network change.

Discovery: a client does not know a server speaks h3, so it first connects with h2 over TCP, the server answers with an Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 header (or the HTTPS DNS record), and the client upgrades next time, racing both.

Comparison.

HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
Transport TCP TCP QUIC over UDP
Parallelism 6 connections multiplexed streams multiplexed streams
HOL blocking HTTP + TCP TCP only none across streams
Header compression none HPACK QPACK
New connection (with TLS 1.3) 2 RTT 2 RTT 1 RTT (0-RTT resume)
Survives IP change no no yes

Industry examples. Google, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and Cloudflare serve h3 widely; Nginx (1.25+), Envoy, Caddy and CloudFront support it. Gains are biggest on lossy mobile links, small on fast wired links.

Decision gravity. Turn on at the edge/CDN: low risk, reversible. Do not make business logic depend on it. Keep h2 and h1 working as fallback.

Everyday analogy. The same delivery menu (HTTP) but a better courier service (QUIC) that handles each parcel separately and follows you when you move house.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing HTTP/3 changes API semantics or needs code changes.
  • Forgetting UDP 443 must be open and fallback exists.
  • Claiming h3 is always faster; on clean networks the difference is small and CPU is higher.

notes.title: Choosing a protocol and connection settings
notes.html:
Decision guide for a designer.

  • Public web/mobile API: terminate h2/h3 at a CDN or L7 load balancer; origin can be h1.1 or h2.
  • Service to service, high volume: gRPC (h2) with client-side or L7 load balancing; or HTTP/1.1 with a keep-alive pool for simplicity.
  • Real time with bi-directional data: WebSocket (over h1.1 upgrade) or WebTransport (h3) or SSE.
  • Live media or games: UDP / WebRTC / QUIC.
  • Plain queries and metrics at massive scale: UDP fire-and-forget (StatsD), accepting loss.

Connection tuning knobs worth knowing (typical values):

# Typical settings to align (illustrative)
client_idle_timeout: 45s        # must be < server/LB idle timeout
alb_idle_timeout: 60s           # AWS ALB default
server_keepalive_timeout: 75s   # nginx keepalive_timeout is a common value
max_connections_per_host: 50    # HTTP client pool
connect_timeout: 1s
read_timeout: 3s
tcp_keepalive: 30s

Production incident pattern. Sporadic connection reset or 502 on idle clients: server/LB closed an idle connection and the client reused it. Metric: spike of 502/504 and connection reset by peer after quiet periods. Fix: client idle timeout < LB idle timeout, enable retry on idempotent requests.

Another pattern: connection storm after a deploy: every client reconnects at once, doing TCP + TLS handshakes together and saturating CPU. Fix: jitter, connection draining, gradual rollout.

Industry examples. Google uses QUIC at the edge and internal RPC (Stubby/gRPC) inside. Cloudflare terminates h3 at the edge and speaks h1/h2 to origins. Uber moved mobile traffic to QUIC for tail-latency gains.

Everyday analogy. Choose transport like a vehicle: lorry (TCP) for guaranteed freight, motorbike (UDP) for fast light deliveries where a lost one does not matter, and a modern courier (QUIC) for both.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing a protocol without saying the network conditions (mobile versus data centre).
  • No timeouts at all: unbounded waits exhaust threads (always set connect and read timeouts).
  • Mismatched idle timeouts between client, LB and server.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• TCP: reliable ordered byte stream, 1 RTT handshake, flow control (receiver), congestion control (network, slow start), but head-of-line blocking and IP-tied connections.
  • UDP: no handshake, order or retransmit; right for DNS, voice, games, metrics, and as the base for QUIC.
  • QUIC: UDP-based, TLS 1.3 built in, 1-RTT/0-RTT setup, independent streams, connection migration; costs CPU and needs TCP fallback.
  • HTTP/1.1: one request per connection at a time, 6 connections per host; HTTP/2: multiplexed streams on one TCP connection, HPACK; HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC with QPACK.
  • Latency is round trips: fresh TCP+TLS1.3 = 2 RTT, QUIC = 1 RTT, resumed 0-RTT. Reuse connections.
  • Use h2/h3 at the edge, gRPC or pooled h1.1 inside; align idle timeouts (client < LB < server) and always set connect/read timeouts.
